about.title: Folsom Product Liability Claims
about.longDescription: A defective product can hurt someone in Folsom without any warning. A space heater shorts out overnight. An e-bike brake gives way on a neighborhood path. A faulty airbag or tire fails during a routine drive down Iron Point Road or E Bidwell Street, turning an ordinary errand into one of the 80 injury collisions Folsom recorded in 2025. When that happens, California law puts the burden where it belongs. Under strict liability, you generally do not have to prove the manufacturer was careless. What matters is whether the product had a design, manufacturing, or warning defect, and whether that defect caused your injury. Manufacturers, distributors, and the store that sold the item may all share responsibility. LawProactive is not a law firm. We are a free service that connects Folsom residents with an independent personal injury attorney who handles product cases on contingency, so there is no fee unless there is a recovery. Keep the product, keep the packaging, and reach out when you are ready.

items.title: Strict Liability Explained Simply
items.desc: In California, you usually need to show the product was defective and that the defect caused your harm, not that anyone was negligent. The attorney we connect you with can walk through how that applies to your situation.

items.question: I was hurt when a part failed on my car near Iron Point Road. Is that a car accident case or a product case?
items.answer: It can be both. Folsom logged 113 people injured in traffic collisions in 2025, and some of those involve equipment that did not perform as it should have. If a defective tire, brake, or airbag contributed to your injuries, a product liability claim against the manufacturer may exist alongside any claim involving another driver. Have the vehicle inspected before it is repaired or scrapped so the evidence is not lost.

items.question: Do I need to prove the manufacturer did something wrong?
items.answer: Generally, no. California applies strict liability to most product defect claims, meaning the focus is on whether the product had a design, manufacturing, or warning defect and whether that defect caused your injury. The company's level of care is usually not the question. That said, each case has its own facts, so it helps to talk with an attorney about yours.

items.question: Should I throw away the product that hurt me?
items.answer: Please don't. The product itself is often the most important piece of evidence in a defect claim, along with its packaging, instructions, and any receipt. Store it somewhere safe and avoid trying to repair or alter it. Photographs of the item and your injuries are also helpful to share with the attorney you're connected with.
